Wisk was founded in 2010 as Zee Aero and in 2017 merged with Larry Page-backed Kitty Hawk before being rebranded as Cora, the name of one of the company’s early air taxi prototypes.
In 2019, Kitty Hawk partnered with Boeing to further develop Cora and spun off the company under the Wisk Aero banner.
Per a Securities and Exchange Commission filing, Boeing will have a seat on Archer’s board so long as it retains at least 10 percent ownership of the company’s stock. Notably, a technology sharing agreement would give Boeing continued access to Wisk’s core autonomous flight technology for its current and next-generation aircraft.

### [Archer to acquire Boeing's Wisk Aero, Insitu and SkyGrid](https://www.ventureatlas.org/news/2026-08-10-archer-acquires-boeing-wisk-insitu-skygrid)  
Archer Aviation signed a definitive agreement on August 10 to acquire three Boeing subsidiaries, autonomous eVTOL developer Wisk Aero, defense drone maker Insitu, and airspace-management software firm SkyGrid, in a deal expected to close by year-end pending antitrust review. Boeing will receive Archer Class A shares and warrants giving it a stake of nearly 20% in Archer, plus the right to invest up to $55 million in an upcoming Archer funding round, while retaining cross-licensing rights to Wisk's autonomous flight systems for its own commercial and defense platforms.

results.name: Archer Aviation acquires rival Wisk Aero from Boeing in landmark deal - Innovation Village | Technology, Product Reviews, Business
results.content:
In a dramatic shift within the advanced air mobility sector, electric vertical takeoff and landing (eVTOL) developer Archer Aviation has acquired its former rival [Wisk Aero,](https://wisk.aero/) alongside two other high-profile aerospace subsidiaries, from [The Boeing Company.](https://innovation-village.com/boeing-whistleblower-curtis-ewbank-says-737-changes-are-not-enough/)  
The deal comes three years after the two companies settled a contentious trade secret lawsuit, fully cementing a dramatic transition from legal adversaries to strategic corporate allies.
### **From Lawsuits to Consolidation: The Legal Backstory**  
The transaction marks the culmination of an intense and publicly bitter corporate dispute:  
- **April 2021 (The Lawsuit):**Wisk Aero filed a high-profile lawsuit against Archer, alleging “brazen theft” of trade secrets, confidential software, and proprietary intellectual property.
- **The Counter-Suit:**Archer aggressively denied the allegations and launched a**$1 billion countersuit**against Wisk, alleging trade defamation and anti-competitive practices.
- **August 2023 (The Settlement):**The two companies reached a surprise resolution. Beyond dropping all legal claims, Archer designated Wisk as its exclusive provider for future autonomous flight systems and granted Wisk stock warrants to acquire up to**13.17 million shares**of Archer common stock at $0.01 per share.
### **The Origins and Evolution of Wisk Aero**  
Wisk’s roots trace back to Kittyhawk, an early electric aviation enterprise co-founded by Sebastian Thrun (former head of Alphabet’s X division) and financed by Google co-founder Larry Page.  
While Kittyhawk developed several experimental aircraft, including the single-seater *Flyer* and the autonomous *Heaviside* prototype, its two-person autonomous air taxi project, codenamed Cora, became the company’s core asset.

results.name: Archer acquires Wisk Aero and two other Boeing subsidiaries - electrive.com
results.content:
# Archer acquires Wisk Aero and two other Boeing subsidiaries  
The transaction encompasses three distinct companies which together account for nearly two million flight hours: Wisk Aero, SkyGrid, and Insitu. The deal is expected to close by the end of 2026 and remains subject to regulatory approvals. Financial details, including the purchase price and the extent of Boeing’s future stake in Archer, have not been disclosed.  
As reported by *Aerotelegraph*, Archer’s core eVTOL business is central to the deal – particularly where Wisk Aero is concerned. Wisk Aero has spent 16 years developing autonomous eVTOLs and has completed over 1,700 test flights, according to its records. While Archer’s own eVTOL, Midnight, will initially operate with a pilot, the acquisition of Wisk lays the technology groundwork for future autonomous operations to the company. SkyGrid, meanwhile, provides software for automated air traffic management, supporting the integration of autonomous and unmanned aerial vehicles into airspace.  
Archer and Wisk share a history: [In 2021,](https://www.electrive.net/2021/04/16/wisk-aero-verklagt-archer-aviation/) Wisk sued its competitor for alleged theft of trade secrets (*link in German*)[.](https://www.electrive.net/2021/04/16/wisk-aero-verklagt-archer-aviation/) The dispute was settled in 2023, after which Boeing invested in Archer, and the two companies agreed to collaborate on autonomy technologies. Now, Wisk is fully transitioning under Archer’s umbrella.
## Archer expands business beyond eVTOLs  
The acquisition of Insitu adds another dimension to the transaction. The company specialises in unmanned aerial systems, particularly for reconnaissance and surveillance missions. What’s more, it has reportedly delivered over 3,500 systems and is profitable, with annual revenues exceeding $200 million US dollars. This aligns with Archer’s growing focus on defence: since late 2024, the company has collaborated with Anduril on a hybrid VTOL aircraft for military applications and introduced Thunder, an autonomous VTOL aircraft, in July 2026. In parallel, Archer is advancing the commercial use of electric aircraft: in July, the company announced the ACES charging infrastructure consortium alongside BETA Technologies and Macquarie Capital. The consortium aims to equip more than [250 sites across the USA by 2030](https://www.electrive.com/2026/07/21/archer-and-beta-plan-250-charging-sites-for-electric-aircraft/).  
This significantly broadens Archer’s strategy: Midnight remains its flagship electric aircraft, while Wisk and SkyGrid provide autonomy and air traffic management solutions. Insitu contributes an established drone business, and ACES delivers the charging infrastructure. However, the speed at which these elements can be integrated into commercial eVTOL operations still depends on progress in certification and market ramp-up.
Boeing is not fully exiting the picture: a parallel technology partnership ensures the corporation retains access to Wisk’s technologies, and Boeing will also hold a future stake in Archer. Archer describes the combination of autonomy, eVTOLs, drones, and software as the foundation of a ‘Physical AI’ platform for aviation and defence. With this deal, Archer is evolving from a manufacturer primarily focused on electric air taxis into a more diversified aviation company. At the same time, it remains unclear what role the civil eVTOL business will play in the future compared to the growing segment of autonomous and military systems.

### Archer Aviation Acquires Wisk Aero: A New Era in Electric Aviation  
In a surprising twist of fate, Archer Aviation has taken a monumental step in the electric aviation sector by acquiring its former rival, Wisk Aero, just three years after a protracted legal battle over trade secrets. This landmark acquisition not only reshapes the landscape of electric aircraft development but also signals a collaborative spirit between two ambitious companies.
#### Key Details of the Acquisition  
According to a recent regulatory filing, Boeing has agreed to divest Wisk Aero, along with two other subsidiaries—SkyGrid, which specializes in air traffic management software, and drone manufacturer Insitu—to Archer. In exchange, Boeing will receive an ownership stake in Archer, amounting to approximately 19.75% of Archer’s outstanding shares right before the deal’s closure, which translates to around a 16.5% stake post-transaction.  
This acquisition marks a full circle for the relationship between Archer and Wisk, which had been marred by allegations of patent infringement and intellectual property theft. In April 2021, Wisk initiated legal action against Archer, alleging “brazen theft” of proprietary information. After two years of contentious litigation, the two companies reached an unexpected settlement that paved the way for collaboration, with Archer making Wisk the official provider of autonomous technology.
#### From Rivalry to Partnership  
Wisk Aero’s journey began as part of Kittyhawk, an electric aviation startup helmed by Sebastian Thrun and backed by Google co-founder Larry Page. Despite shutting down operations in September 2022, the company’s innovations, including the Cora autonomous flying taxi, were spun off into a joint venture with Boeing, eventually becoming Wisk Aero.  
Boeing heavily invested in Wisk, contributing millions to support its mission of developing electric, self-flying air taxis. By 2023, Wisk had evolved into a fully-owned subsidiary of Boeing, setting the stage for its acquisition by Archer.
